<reason>CON controlled the decision rule from its opening by separating "a room where nobody dies" from the motion's actual promises (city-wide deaths, public disorder) and then harvested a string of PRO concessions: sites capture a "fraction" of injections, the supply is "poisoned everywhere," Latin American deaths averted are "smaller," and there "the second promise does the heavy lifting." PRO's counterfactual/displacement test in A1 was actually a reasonable metric, but the "magic number" phrasing let CON credibly frame it as walking away from the motion's outcome. PRO's Latin America answer conceded most of the deaths half there, and CON's armed-groups/fixed-queue point on the disorder half was never squarely neutralized beyond "dealers already cluster." PRO scored real hits—Q1 forced CON to retreat from "most reversals wouldn't have been fatal," and the "factory that hands out seatbelts" reframe was clever—but CON turned even that in closing ("you argued your way to my alternative: a door and a nurse, not supervised chairs"). CON's opening was clipped, a minor execution cost, but its weighing was consistently sharper and it made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The lifeguard/seatbelt exchange: PRO flipped the lifeguard to "nobody dies because someone is watching," CON re-flipped it to "the room watches a few square meters while swimming happens city-wide," then turned PRO's seatbelt analogy into "a seatbelt bolted to one chair" versus pocket naloxone that rides with the user—directly pressing the motion's city-wide mortality burden and forcing PRO's late shift to a trust/distribution mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
